articles.title: NUJP, journalists lament loss of media watchdog as CMFR writes 30
articles.summary: Media practitioners and journalist groups have conveyed bittersweet messages of sadness and respect as the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) writes 30--an industry term that…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 2:22pm

Media practitioners and journalist groups have conveyed bittersweet messages of sadness and respect as the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) writes 30—an industry term that indicates that a story is complete.
The CMFR announced that it would cease operations on September 30, after 37 years of serving an independently funded vanguard of a free Filipino press.
The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) said it regretted the pending closure of CMFR.
"Its work has helped the press hold power to account while also reminding journalists that the freedom we exercise carries with it a responsibility to the public," the NUJP wrote.

"The loss of a watchdog that watches over the watchdogs is a profound blow to Philippine journalism, leaving a void in an industry that needs accountability. At a time when the press faces mounting pressures from various interests, the absence of CMFR's independent voice will be deeply felt," the union added.
More journalists have also expressed their sorrow following the CMFR's closure, with many lauding CMFR founder Melinda Quintos de Jesus.
Presidential Task Force on Media Security Executive Director Joe Torres, who formerly served as editor-in-chief of GMA News Online, extended his gratitude to the CMFR.

"Started in journalism in 1989, the year CMFR started. The organization has been a great help in the formation of many journalists of my time. Maraming salamat, CMFR, Ma'am Melinda, at sa lahat na mga kaibigan at nakasama sa Center," Torres said in a comment on the post.
Legacy
Former Business World editor-in-chief and now PLDT communications division chief Roby Alampay also lauded the watchdog.

"Your legacy and the impact of Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility will live on. We are all grateful — and now collectively responsible to ensure that it be so. Maraming salamat sa lahat nang bumuo at bumuhay sa CMFR at kanyang adhikain!” Alampay said.
NUJP Chair Jonathan de Santos, who serves as ABS-CBN deputy editor, also thanked the CMFR in a separate statement.

"My informal journ school whose standards I aspire to and sometimes met. Thank you for your decades of service, guidance, praise and scolding, and hope in journalism in the Philippines," De Santos said.
Sports journalist Rey Joble thanked CMFR for standing with him during a plagiarism issue, wherein portions of his work were copied into another article.
“Your legacy lives on. But allow me to thank you, CMFR, for standing by me at the height of my plagiarism issue 15 years ago. It was a life-changing moment,” Joble said.
TV5 journalist Ed Lingao, meanwhile, put it simply: "CMFR writes -30-."
Standing up for rights
Meanwhile, the In Defense of Human Rights and Dignity Movement (iDefend) group expressed sadness over the CMFR's impending closure.
iDEFEND said that the CMFR was there to stand by the truth during former president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody war on drugs.

"Ang inyong pagtindig sa karapatang pantao at demokrasya ay malaking kontribusyon sa pagpapanagot sa nagdaang administrasyon. Mula sa hanay ng iDefend, pagpupugay at pasasalamat CMFR!" the group said.
(Your stance on human rights and democracy was a big contributor to holding the previous administration accountable. From iDefend, recognition and gratitude.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No basis for claim that Bato Dela Rosa is under Trump’s protection
articles.summary: The video merely speculates about the unnamed 'powerful people' whom Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said are allegedly protecting the senator, who remains at large

blocks.text: Claim: Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is under the protection of US President Donald Trump and is currently under American custody.
Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube channel named Update Pinas News, credited to Don Mar TV, uploaded the video on September 10 carrying the claim.

Text on its thumbnail reads, “Iyak sila dito, hawak pala ni Trump” (They’re crying here; it turns out he’s with Trump), with “Bato spotted!” placed over an image showing Trump in a hotel lobby alongside a man resembling Dela Rosa.
The video’s title reads, “Heto na! Big good news mga DDS! Safe na si Bato? Nasa kamay pala ni Trump? Palasyo-Junior nagulantang!”
(Here it is! Big good news, DDS! Is Bato safe? Turns out he’s in Trump’s hands? Palace-Junior stunned!)
The video has garnered over 5,600 views and 250 likes as of writing.
The facts: There is no credible report, government statement, or public remark from Trump confirming that Dela Rosa is under US protection or custody.

There is also no documented interaction showing Trump with Dela Rosa being escorted by, or in the custody of, US authorities. No reports have likewise indicated that Dela Rosa is seeking asylum in the US or any other country.

The video appears to build its claim around actual remarks by Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla. In a September 8 interview, Remulla said authorities knew where Dela Rosa was and were negotiating with people he described as the senator’s “protectors” and “very powerful people.” Remulla did not identify these individuals or say that they were connected to Trump, the United States, or any foreign government.

Remulla also explained that the government was pursuing negotiations to avoid a violent confrontation during the effort to arrest Dela Rosa. He said authorities wanted the senator to surrender peacefully while using legal measures to bring him out of hiding.

Dela Rosa’s lawyer, Israelito Torreon, separately denied having personal knowledge of the alleged protectors. In a September 9 statement, Torreon described dela Rosa as a “prayerful man” whose only protector was God.

The only documented instance in which Dela Rosa called on Trump to intervene was in April 2025, when he urged the US president to consider sanctions against Filipinos involved in the arrest of former president Rodrigo Duterte and his turnover to the International Criminal Court (ICC). He did not make the same appeal for himself or claim that Trump was protecting him from his own ICC arrest warrant.

Where things stand: The Philippine National Police said its efforts to locate and arrest Dela Rosa are ongoing. The senator has been in hiding since May 2026, after he left the Senate following a shooting incident. He is wanted under an ICC arrest warrant in connection with the crimes against humanity case involving Duterte. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

articles.title: Philippines' media watchdog CMFR to close after 37 years
articles.summary: Post-EDSA press freedom watchdog ends 37 years of operations on Sept. 30.

blocks.text: September 18, 2026 | 2:07pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility, a fixture of Philippine journalism's post-dictatorship rebuilding, will shut down on September 30 after 37 years, citing mounting difficulty securing funds for its operations.

CMFR announced the closure Friday, September 18, citing the decision of its board. With it ends the work of one of the country's most established media watchdogs and an institution that helped shape professional and ethical standards in Philippine journalism.

"Philippine and international funding support has sustained the work of CMFR; but multiple factors have affected the funding environment, making it difficult for CMFR to secure the necessary funds for its operations," the organization said.

Established in 1989 by journalist Melinda Quintos de Jesus, three years after the People Power uprising ended the Marcos dictatorship, CMFR was created as the Philippine press rebuilt its freedoms and institutions after 14 years of authoritarian rule.
Its founding premise joined two concerns that would define much of its work: defending press freedom from outside interference while demanding greater responsibility from the press itself.
Over nearly four decades, CMFR became a persistent monitor of both.

It documented killings, threats and attacks against journalists, tracked impunity in media murders and regularly assessed the state of press freedom. At the same time, it scrutinized news coverage for accuracy, fairness, balance, context and sourcing, often publicly calling out lapses by news organizations.

That role placed CMFR in an unusual position in the industry. It defended journalists against repression while arguing that press freedom could be sustained only by stronger professional practice and self-regulation.
Building standards after dictatorship
CMFR began monitoring Philippine media in 1990, developing what became the Philippine Journalism Review and later PJR Reports into vehicles for peer review, accountability and continuing education.

Through media monitoring, training programs and published ethical guidelines, CMFR sought to establish common standards in a profession where routes into journalism, training and newsroom practices varied widely.

Its 2007 ethics manual was published as an effort to further professionalize Philippine journalism, linking ethical practice with competence and laying out guidance on accuracy, conflicts of interest, privacy and coverage of crises, crime, war, terrorism, women and children.

CMFR also organized training for working journalists, developed reporting manuals and established press councils intended to give members of the public a way to raise grievances against media without immediately turning to the courts.

PJR Reports became a regular forum for evaluating the performance of Philippine news organizations and a reference for journalism schools. CMFR described the publication as a mechanism for self-evaluation and correction, and as a model of media self-regulation.

The organization also spent two decades administering the Jaime V. Ongpin Awards for Excellence in Journalism, which recognized investigative and explanatory reporting and helped establish benchmarks for sourcing, verification, fairness, accuracy and technical proficiency.
Its next iteration, the Jaime V. Ongpin Journalism Seminar, annually selects journalists commended for their coverage of critical issues affecting Filipinos.
CMFR's ethics manual and other publications also became reference materials in universities, while its seminars regularly brought working journalists together with students and faculty.
Watching the watchdogs
As a watchdog, CMFR was frequently unsparing toward the industry it sought to protect.
Its media monitoring examined not only attacks on journalists but failures within journalism itself, including weak sourcing, lack of context, sensationalism and ethical lapses.
That combination of advocacy and criticism reflected an argument embedded in CMFR's work since its founding: that the credibility of the press was itself part of the defense of press freedom.
The organization also became a repository of data on attacks against journalists.

Its reports, often produced with other media organizations and press-freedom groups, documented journalist killings, legal harassment, red-tagging, surveillance, censorship and other threats across successive administrations.
CMFR's reports and alerts also circulated through international press-freedom networks, giving its documentation a role beyond the Philippine media industry.
An institution of the post-1986 press

The organization's lifespan covered markedly different periods for the Philippine press, from the democratic opening after Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s dictatorship through successive political crises, the rise of digital media, the collapse of traditional advertising models and renewed pressure on journalists.
CMFR described those 37 years as a mission carried out through "widely differing political environments and the diverse challenges they presented."

Its closure comes as the economics supporting journalism and media-development institutions have grown more difficult, while Philippine news organizations continue to face questions of financial sustainability, safety and public trust.

In its farewell statement, CMFR and its executive director thanked its past and present staff, journalists and news organizations, embassies, schools, students and civil society groups that had supported its work.
"We are truly grateful," De Jesus said. "Please accept our best wishes."

articles.title: Revealed: How Russia use mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizens
articles.summary:
Research shows tens of millions of people are being forced to use platform that amounts to ‘backdoor’ on their device

Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced…

blocks.text: Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max.

Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app.
It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max.

Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls.
But while WeChat was developed over decades, in step with China’s other internet controls, Max has been imposed on a population that once had mostly-free internet access.

blocks.caption: Max is described as ‘a blueprint any government can follow’ towards digital authoritarianism. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images

blocks.text: Now, forensic research has revealed a fuller picture of Max’s powerful surveillance capabilities. These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan.

“We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens.
Max is “a blueprint any government can follow” towards digital authoritarianism, said Ensafi.
It represents the cutting edge of what governments such as Iran, Kazakhstan and India may soon try to achieve.

Ensafi’s team were able to download the version of the app used in Russia. They found that Max can screenshot users’ devices – and the contents of its mini-apps – without their knowledge. It can access all the information stored in these mini-apps, their messages and payments. It can impersonate its users without them knowing.
It can even inject code into mini-apps – which would mean, said Ensafi, that the Russian government could use Max to launch cyberattacks.

Their research adds new clarity into an ongoing debate on Max’s surveillance capabilities. Crucially, said Ensafi, it cannot break into apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, if users have these installed. However, Russia has banned both.

Many Russians working in or around state institutions have in effect been forced to use Max. Officials and public-sector employees, university students, teachers and even schoolchildren have all faced pressure to move their communications on to the platform.
One schoolteacher in Moscow said staff at their school were ordered to switch to Max after instructions from the city authorities.

“The school director called us in last March and told us directly: from now on, everything is on Max. That included chats with parents, sending out homework and other school communication,” the teacher said.
“There isn’t really an option to say no, so in the end you just use the app,” they added.

blocks.caption: The Russian State Duma deputy, Sergey Boyarsky, demonstrating an age verification system using the Max app at a supermarket in February. Photograph: Contributor/Getty Images

blocks.text: Daniil, a university student in St Petersburg, said he reluctantly downloaded Max shortly before the start of the academic year after being told students would be denied access to university buildings or dormitories without a QR code generated through the app.
He said he had concerns about the app’s security and privacy, but felt he had little choice if he wanted to continue accessing campus.

Among Russia’s elite, use of Max often appears to be largely performative, with Telegram and Signal still widely used for day-to-day communication, according to several well-connected figures and prominent businesspeople.
One person in the Kremlin’s inner circle said he and several friends had bought second phones solely to install Max, while continuing to use their main devices and preferred messaging apps as before.
“It’s all for show. No one in politics really uses it,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Max has yet to replace Telegram as a major source of news for Russians. Public channels – used by media outlets, bloggers and officials to broadcast news and commentary to large audiences – remain far less developed on Max, where only a small number have built audiences comparable to the biggest channels on Telegram.

Several Max users contacted by the Guardian said the app closely resembles Telegram, long Russia’s most popular messaging platform, in its design and functionality, but concerns about privacy and surveillance were widespread.
“Using Max feels like you never quite know who else might be watching,” said Nikolai, a 34-year-old consultant in Moscow.
While the app looked modern and slick, Nikolai said there was always something slightly sinister about using it.
“You end up using it more and more because the alternatives are becoming harder to access. But it still doesn’t feel right.”

Russia’s success in rapidly pushing out Max should be a “wake-up call”, said Ensafi. China reached its current state of digital authoritarianism over the course of 35 years. But Russia has imposed these sweeping restrictions – shepherding people on to a state-controlled internet – in just a decade.
“The world is changing, the infrastructure of private communication is changing – and the assault by authoritarian governments is very aggressive,” she said.
Max and VKontakte were approached for comment.

articles.title: Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir
articles.summary:
Peer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq Khan

Another former government minister has been hired by a…

blocks.text: Another former government minister has been hired by a controversial US AI company, this time Palantir, which has appointed Andy Burnham’s former ministerial colleague Tom Watson.

The Labour peer and former deputy leader will operate alongside Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, as the company attempts to fend off pressure on Burnham’s government to axe its £330m NHS contract. It is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the Labour London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. Palantir also wants to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m.

The company was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and provides AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. Alex Karp, its chief executive, said: “This is just the latest chapter of Tom’s forty-year fight for better public services. We are fortunate to have him guide us as we help the British government to deliver for the British public.”
after newsletter promotion
His job will be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”, Palantir said.

Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, Watson has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir, including accompanying Mosley at Labour party conferences. He was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Palantir has a £240m contract with the Ministry of Defence.

The move is just the latest example of a revolving door between British politics and big tech. After the former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg spent nearly seven years earning millions working for Mark Zuckerberg at Meta, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak last year took jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft and the former chancellor George Osborne started working for OpenAI. Keir Starmer’s AI adviser, Matt Clifford, also joined Anthropic this month. He tried to retain the chair of a government science and tech research body, but quit under pressure over conflicts of interest.

“The revolving door is proving very fruitful for big tech,” said Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group. “The only surefire way to stop tech companies benefiting from privileged information acquired by ministers or senior civil servants is to introduce an enforceable five-year ban on taking up industry posts.”

Watson said he was “terrifically excited” by the new role as Palantir’s senior vice-president and highlighted two of the contracts that are in dispute when he said he wanted to help Palantir speed up NHS diagnosis, treatment and discharge from hospitals and enable “our police to crack crimes and root out corruption”. Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while working for Palantir in London.

articles.title: Chinese vessel rams PH ship on fuel subsidy mission near Palawan
articles.summary: Chinese vessel rams PH ship on fuel subsidy mission near Palawan

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 1:56pm

A China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel rammed a Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) ship that was delivering fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.
PCG spokesperson for WPS Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said CCG vessel 21585 rammed the BRP Datu Magat Salamat while the Philippine vessel was carrying out its maritime patrol and fuel subsidy mission.
Tarriela said that at 11:04 a.m., the Chinese vessel reportedly cut across the stern of the BFAR vessel at a distance of only about 10 meters.
At 11:13 a.m., while the BRP Datu Magat Salamat was maintaining its course, the Chinese vessel repeated the maneuver and made contact with the BFAR vessel, striking it.

A China Coast Guard (CCG) vessel rammed a Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) ship that was delivering fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on Friday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said. 🎥: PCG @gmanews pic.twitter.com/5F8jzM7t9H— Joviland Rita (@jovilandxrita) September 18, 2026

The Philippine vessel sustained damage on its starboard side including the bent, broken, and detached; deformed metal stanchions and support structures deformed; and displaced deck fixtures and equipment displaced, with debris scattered across the deck.
After the collision, CCG-21585 conducted another dangerous maneuver, passing dead astern at a distance of only about five meters, according to Tarriela.
GMA News Online has reached out to the Chinese Embassy for comment but it has yet to reply as of posting time.
The incident occurred around 6.36 nautical miles north-northwest of Abad Santos Shoal and about 54 nautical miles from Palawan's coast, within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan has directed PCG surface and air assets to proceed to the location of the BFAR vessel to provide assistance and ensure the safety of its crew.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: South Korea will not send military to support US war on Iran, defying Trump pressure
articles.summary:
Seoul resolves recent speculation over sending military to strait of Hormuz, saying ‘there won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war’

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has…

blocks.text: South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will ⁠not deploy the military to the ⁠Middle East in a way ​that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a ⁠news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”

However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to ​protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of ‌our people,” he said.

Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war ‌and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a ‌possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.

Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed ‌a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.

The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed ​to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.

North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

articles.title: ‘We have something that will kill Elliott’: Icac questions former Labor councillor over message
articles.summary: Sharangan Maheswaran denies message he received about NSW minister was related to work for fugitive property developer

blocks.text: A former Labor councillor says he had a “common interest” with a conservative Liberal operative, but denied that a message he received about damaging the reputation of NSW Liberal minister David Elliot was related to political work for a fugitive property developer, an inquiry has heard.

Sharangan Maheswaran told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that a message sent to him by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood claiming “We have something that will kill Elliott” did not relate to work by Greenwood’s company Beckington for Jean Nassif.

Icac is investigating whether Maheswaran and fellow Labor Strathfield councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct towards former mayor Matthew Blackmore in a way “that involves the dishonest or partial exercise of their official functions and/or a breach of public trust, including conduct which could involve blackmail” and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act. Maheswaran has denied any wrongdoing.

Maheswaran, who is no longer a councillor, was a lawyer to property developer Nassif and became an executive at his company, Toplace, in September 2020. He has also denied wrongdoing in relation to a separate allegation under investigation by Icac.

Icac is examining whether Liberal figures Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis anticipated receiving $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes, including damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister and centre-right faction member David Elliott, who had opposed Toplace developments. Greenwood, Perrottet and Nassif have denied that Nassif paid for political outcomes.
On Friday, Dwyer took Maheswaran to a message Greenwood wrote to him in February 2020 in which he said: “We have something that will kill Elliot.”

Maheswaran replied: “Your ears must be ringing. I just picked up the phone to let you know that I’ve got something decent, and the SMH [Sydney Morning Herald] is going to fire up re [centre-right Liberal MP Alex] Hawke this week off the back of an ALP bill to ban developers.”
Dwyer put it to Maheswaran that the messages showed he shared “a common interest with Beckington in terms of damaging the reputation of David Elliott”.
Maheswaran said he “had a common interest with Mr Greenwood in relation to the Hawke faction of the Liberal party”, but rejected the suggestion the messages related to work by Beckington for Nassif.

The inquiry heard that Maheswaran came to know Nassif through his daughter Ashlyn Nassif, who was sentenced to a six-month community corrections order earlier this month after pleading guilty to providing false or misleading information to obtain a $150m construction loan from Westpac.
Maheswaran said he was subcontracted to do work for Toplace through Ashlyn Nassif and her sister Evelyn Helou’s law firm EA Legal in late 2019, through another company, Anwalt Pty Ltd.
But he took issue with Dwyer’s suggestion that he and Anwalt were one and the same.

He said: “That’s nonsensical from a corporation’s perspective, from a commercial perspective, from any sort of understanding of contractual law, I’m sorry, Dr Dwyer, I’m speaking in terms of as I understand the world.”
“No problem,” replied Dwyer. Under questioning, Maheswaran accepted that he was the only shareholder and employee of Anwalt at the time.
after newsletter promotion
Dwyer said: “So the only person doing any actual work was you, correct?”
“At that point in time, yes,” said Maheswaran.

Maheswaran has been mentioned frequently by other witnesses, and has attended the commission in person while others have given evidence. When Icac announced its public hearings, Maheswaran told Guardian Australia: “I have every confidence that my actions will be regarded by the public and by any fair tribunal to be lawful and entirely in the public interest.”
Greenwood has previously told the commission Maheswaran helped him arrange a private security guard to avoid summons to a parliamentary inquiry that preceded Icac’s inquiry.

Greenwood said he suggested to Maheswaran that Toplace cover the cost for Jean-Claude Perrottet, younger brother of the former premier, to go to Fiji to avoid the inquiry, saying: “You know, your boss is the cause of this, so you can cover it.”
Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
The inquiry continues.

articles.title: PCG: Chinese vessels seen in Bajo de Masinloc as PH distributes aid to fishers
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said Friday several Chinese vessels were spotted during the recent distribution of fuel subsidy and food packs to Filipino fishermen at Bajo de Masinloc, also known…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 1:40pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said Friday several Chinese vessels were spotted during the recent distribution of fuel subsidy and food packs to Filipino fishermen at Bajo de Masinloc, also known as Scarborough Shoal.
In a statement, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said the following Chinese ships were seen Thursday in the area:

items: one People's Liberation Army Navy (PLA-N) warship
three China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels
three Chinese maritime militia vessels

blocks.text: Tarriela said the Chinese warship issued a radio challenge to the PCG's Piper Navajo aircraft, which responded by asserting that it was conducting a lawful maritime patrol within Philippine maritime zones, in accordance with international law.

"The continued presence of Chinese maritime forces in and around BDM, a traditional fishing ground of Filipino fisherfolk, remains inconsistent with the 2016 Arbitral Award and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)," Tarriela said.
"The Award affirmed that Bajo de Masinloc is a traditional fishing ground of Filipino fishermen and that China unlawfully prevented them from fishing there," he added.

Tarriela said the PCG conducted a maritime domain awareness flight over Bajo de Masinloc in support of the ongoing Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda mission led by the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR).
A total of 35 Filipino fishing boats were sighted to receive diesel and food packs.
Bajo de Masinloc is located 124 nautical miles off Masinloc, Zambales, and is considered within the Philippines' 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country's claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. — VDV, GMA News

“Maybe not in the NBI because he might say I am unfair, but there are other government agencies he can go to,” Matibag added.

“On my wife, I’m sure my wife is capable enough to answer allegations. If he, indeed, has evidence against my wife, I encourage him, as a law-abiding citizen, as a member of the House of Representatives, to file a complaint,” Matibag said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: PCG: China Coast Guard ship rams BFAR vessel off Palawan
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine fisheries ship delivering subsidized fuel to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea on Friday, damaging the vessel about…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine fisheries ship delivering subsidized fuel to Filipino fishermen in the West Philippine Sea on Friday, damaging the vessel about 100 kilometers off Palawan, according to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).
The PCG said China Coast Guard vessel CCG-21585 struck the starboard side of BRP Datu Magat Salamat, a Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel, around 11:13 a.m.
The incident occurred near Abad Santos Shoal while the BFAR vessel was on a fuel subsidy mission for Filipino fishermen, the Coast Guard said.
According to the PCG, the Chinese vessel first cut across the stern of BRP Datu Magat Salamat around 11:04 a.m., coming within about 10 meters of the Philippine ship.
Nine minutes later, while the BFAR vessel was maintaining its course, CCG-21585 repeated the maneuver and made contact with it, the PCG said.

blocks.caption: Damaged railings and deck fixtures are seen aboard the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources’ BRP Datu Magat Salamat after it was struck by a China Coast Guard vessel in the West Philippine Sea on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. Photo courtesy of PCG

blocks.text: The collision bent, broke or detached portions of the BFAR vessel’s main railings and deformed metal stanchions and support structures on its starboard side.
Deck fixtures and equipment were also displaced, with debris scattered across the deck, according to an initial damage assessment by the Coast Guard.
The PCG said the Chinese vessel later made another maneuver and passed about five meters behind BRP Datu Magat Salamat.
The incident occurred about 11.8 kilometers north-northwest of Abad Santos Shoal and 100 kilometers from the coast of Palawan, according to the PCG.
Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan ordered PCG surface and air assets to proceed to the area to assist the BFAR vessel and ensure the safety of its crew.
The Coast Guard described the collision as deliberate and accused the Chinese vessel of endangering the Filipino crew.
There was no immediate information from the PCG on injuries among the crew.
BRP Datu Magat Salamat was the same vessel that ran aground at Hasa-Hasa Shoal on Thursday while approaching Filipino fishing boats to distribute fuel.
BRP Malabrigo of the Philippine Coast Guard pulled the vessel free later that day after fishing boats initially failed to refloat it due to low tide and limited towing power.
The PCG also monitored a China Coast Guard aircraft conducting what it described as “apparent aerial surveillance” over the grounded vessel while the salvage operation was underway.
Beijing claims sovereignty over islands and maritime rights across nearly the entire South China Sea, including areas within the West Philippine Sea.
In 2016, an arbitral tribunal ruled that there was no legal basis for China’s claim to historic rights to resources within the sea areas falling inside its so-called nine-dash line.
China has rejected the ruling and maintains that it is “null and void.” /mr

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Davao City received funds from nat’l government under Marcos admin
articles.summary: Malacañang said Davao City received national government support for programs and projects, citing data from the budget department

blocks.text: Claim: Davao City did not receive any funds from the national government under the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook page named “Wing Jusayan Vlog” posted the claim on August 22. The post featured images of Marcos and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte.

Text overlaid on the graphic reads: “Davao City survived without funds in 4 years, why are you looking for the project that was not funded by government? The worst part inangkin nyo ang project na hindi naman sa inyo (you took credit for the project that wasn’t yours).”

As of writing, the post garnered over 11,000 reactions, 2,300 comments, and 5,400 shares. Similar posts bearing the same claim are also circulating online. Several commenters, believing the claim, further asserted that Davao City has good leadership and governance while shaming the national government for supposedly withholding funds.
The claim appears to stem from Duterte’s comments that the city allegedly received no funding from the national government for years.
The facts: Davao City received yearly funding from the national government, according to Malacañang, citing records from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).

In a statement, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that Davao City and its barangays received a combined P53.11 billion in national tax allotment (NTA) and other national government allocations from fiscal years (FY) 2022 to 2026, as reported by the Philippine News Agency on September 4. This contradicts the misleading posts’ claim that Davao City received “no funds” over a four-year period.

Of that total, approximately P41.63 billion went directly to the city government, while P11.17 billion was the combined NTA of the city’s barangays. There was also an additional P314.48 million that came from releases under the General Appropriations Act.

Malacañang, through Castro, had previously refuted similar allegations during a May 25 press briefing, explicitly denying claims made by Duterte that the city received zero funds from the national government.
Castro presented an official statement from the DBM that said Duterte’s claim “is not supported by the national government’s released data.”

The DBM records, according to the Palace press officer, show that from FY 2023 to 2026, as of May 17, Davao City received at least P7.856 billion in total national government financial support for its programs and projects. This includes national tax allotment, special shares, fire code fees, and regular operating requirements.Moreover, Castro said that the P7.440 billion came from identified national government agency programs and projects for health, education, infrastructure, and transport modernization projects.

In addition to regular national funding allocations, Rappler also reported that Davao City held the largest confidential budget among all local government units (LGUs) in Southern Mindanao for 2023 and 2024, amounting to P1.06 billion.

Lack of context: On September 6, Duterte clarified that he was specifically referring to the alleged lack of congressional district allocation. In an interview and report by GMA News Online, Castro explained that her refutation of Duterte’s claim was made in response to specific inquiries regarding “the NTA allotment, her assessment of the claim that Davao City had received no funds from the national government, and whether there were pertinent records to support the claim.”Under Article X, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, local government units are legally guaranteed a just share of national government revenues, which must be automatically released directly to LGUs.
Debunked: Rappler has debunked a similar claim associating the supposed non-release of government funds to political reasons. – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com
Lyndee Buenagua is journalist based in Baguio and Bicol, and an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Philippine media watchdog CMFR is closing
articles.summary: CMFR will close on September 30, its executive director Melinda Quintos de Jesus says

blocks.text: CMFR will close on September 30, its executive director Melinda Quintos de Jesus says
MANILA, Philippines – For nearly four decades, the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) stood as a watchdog over the watchdogs of Philippine democracy.
It will close on September 30, its executive director Melinda Quintos de Jesus said.
The decision was not about the work, but about whether there were enough resources left to keep doing it.
The CMFR board made the decision after confronting a funding environment that had become increasingly difficult, Quintos de Jesus said.

For years, Philippine and international funders had financed the center’s work. But that support had become harder to secure, leaving the organization without the resources required to continue operating.

The CMFR, for 37 years, had occupied a distinctive place in Philippine journalism. It had examined the conduct of the media even as it defended the press against those who sought to intimidate or silence it.

It also documented attacks and threats against journalists and news organizations, promoted media ethics, honored excellence in journalism, trained reporters to cover women, children and minority groups, as well as disasters, elections, and periods of political and social crises.

The closing of the center thus marks the disappearance of an institution whose work was, in part, to remember what happened to Philippine journalism – who was threatened, who was attacked, how the press responded, and what standards were expected of those who wielded its power.
In announcing the decision, Quintos de Jesus thanked those who had supported CMFR’s undertakings. – with a report from Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

articles.title: What is in the EU’s planned KIDS Act?
articles.summary: Here are the details of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which will require approval from European Union governments and the European Parliament and could be revised before it is enacted

blocks.text: EU AND SOCIAL MEDIA. An EU flag and smartphone with displayed social media app icons in this illustration taken February 3, 2026
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Here are the details of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which will require approval from European Union governments and the European Parliament and could be revised before it is enacted

items: The European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act, which bans social media accounts for children under 13 and allows parent-supervised accounts for those aged 13 and 14.
The Act mandates that social media platforms implement safety measures for users under 18, including bans on addictive features and ensuring children's profiles are private by default.
The legislation aims to standardize child protection rules across EU countries, replacing existing national regulations with a unified approach.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The European Commission has proposed banning under-13s from social media and requiring platforms to design online services that are safe for all children’s accounts.
Here are the details of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which will require approval from European Union governments and the European Parliament and could be revised before it is enacted.

The proposed regulation bans social media accounts for those aged under 13, allows parent-supervised “mini accounts” for children aged 13 and 14, and independent accounts only for those 15 years and older.

For 13- and 14-year-olds, a guardian would be able to set up a limited account that the guardian will control, with a daily limit of up to an hour of age-appropriate social media and video-sharing platforms.

For teenagers with existing accounts, platforms would have to check — within six months of the rules applying — whether existing account holders will have to disable the accounts of children under 15 or for those whose age cannot be established.
Checks would not be required if platforms can tell with high confidence that users are adults.
Age will be verified with certified solutions independent of platforms, including a planned European Digital Identity Wallet.
The EU KIDS Act sets obligations for all social media, video sharing, online video games, AI companions, and chatbots for users below the age of 18.

These include bans on addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds and personalised ads or algorithms based on past activity. The Act would prevent infinite scrolling without breaks, reward ‘tricks’, unsolicited contact from strangers and push notifications during sleeping hours, defined as eight consecutive hours between 10 pm and 8 am.
AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default. Profiles for children must be private by default, with geolocation, camera and microphone access turned off.

The burden of proof will be on platforms to show they are safe for children. Platforms with 45 million or more active monthly users in the EU will have to present compliance plans before coming into contact with children.
The provisions of the EU Kids Act are designed to replace a patchwork of different rules in separate EU countries with the same level of protection across the bloc.

France has pushed for an EU-wide ban for under-15s after France’s Constitutional Court struck down a national bill before it was due to take effect in September, saying it infringed on freedom of expression. – Rappler.com

PISA data show that 47.2% or nearly half of 15-year-old Filipino students reported experiencing “at least one form of bullying a few times per month or more.”
It was more than double the 20% average rate of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the institution behind PISA.
Around three out of 10 Filipino students or 31% were also considered “frequently bullied.”
Who are more likely to report being bullied in the Philippines? Here are the PISA 2025 results:

items: Boys than girls
Disadvantaged students than advantaged students

Located in rural areas or villages than towns or cities
From public schools than private schools

blocks.text: In 2025, the Philippines was no longer the country with the highest index of exposure to bullying, but it still ranked third, following Rwanda and Kenya. It was the first time the two African nations participated in PISA.

The Philippines had been dubbed the world’s “bullying capital”, as noted by observers including the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2), due to its results in global assessments like PISA.

Still, the Department of Education (DepEd) said “there are encouraging signs of improvement,” as it compared the findings from the country’s first PISA participation in 2018, rather than the COVID-19 pandemic era in 2022.
In 2018, 64.9% of Filipino students reported experiencing an act of bullying at least a few times a month or more.
Comparing the 2018 and 2025 PISA cycles, there were declines in reports of students being made fun of by other students, being hit or pushed, being threatened, and being victims of nasty rumors.
PISA results also showed 13.9% of Filipino students reported being cyberbullied in 2025. It was the second highest among participating countries, just behind Rwanda’s 21.7%.
It was way beyond the OECD average of 3%.
PISA asked students if “upsetting” information about them had been published online, without their consent, at least a few times a month during the year prior to the exam.
The report also found that students who spend more time on digital devices are more likely to report incidents of cyberbullying.

“Although cyberbullying is less frequently reported than other forms of bullying, it often occurs in addition to other forms of bullying, and research suggests that it is associated with poorer well-being and mental health outcomes,” the OECD warned.
According to the assessment, cyberbullying victims also tend to experience significant achievement deficits.
In the Philippines, those who were cyberbullied scored 49 points lower in science than their peers, on average.

blocks.caption: Philippines’ reading, math, science scores improve in 2025 PISA

blocks.text: Cyberbullying is also being tracked by the DepEd in its anti-bullying campaign.
However, if the self-reported rates in PISA results are to be believed, the figures are quite distant from what the agency has recorded. Is bullying still “underreported” in the country?
The emphasis on mental health is even greater now following two fatal school shootings this year.

“The current goal of the DepEd is to…foster a more safe and welcoming environment for our students. It should not only be academic. They (the students) should look forward to school, to seeing friends and teachers, and look forward to that day’s lesson,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a news conference after the PISA results announcement on September 8.
Education Undersecretary Carmela Oracion also said the DepEd does not want to be reactive when it comes to school violence.

“There are urgent things to do like [strengthening] the security measures. But apart from that, we want to bring this in through values education…. We are really strengthening that,” she told reporters.
As it stands, it would be an uphill battle for the DepEd amid lack of funding to address the shortage of security guards, CCTV cameras, and metal detectors in public schools.
The agency’s proposed 2027 budget also lacks allocations to train teachers in spotting red flags in student behavior, as well as to fully implement its mental health and counseling program.

The DepEd already signed the revised implementing rules and regulations of the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013 in August 2025, to provide clearer definitions of bullying, set the responsibilities of various sectors, and strengthen school-level response. Budget constraints, however, could be another obstacle. – Rappler.com

articles.title: MPs urge ministers to break off Thames Water talks with US hedge funds
articles.summary:
Efra committee calls for emergency legislation enabling government to take public control of the company

Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company.

Adding their voices to demands that the prime minister takes public control of the company, which has debts of £20bn and is being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors, the MPs said in a report that ministers should consider emergency legislation to take control of its financial affairs to stabilise the company.

Alistair Carmichael, the chair of the environment, food and rural affairs committee (Efra), said it was unbelievable that the special administration regime (SAR) for insolvent or failing water companies could not be triggered for Thames Water on performance grounds alone.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has suggested that an SAR – effectively temporary public control – cannot be triggered under the current law because of the way the US hedge funds that bought Thames Water’s debt have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its liabilities.
The report said Ofwat and the government should withdraw from negotiating with the consortium of distressed-debt specialists who lacked the proper expertise to turn around a vital public service.
Carmichael said the creditors were operating in an opaque way, seeking relief from environmental penalties and dragging out negotiations while reaping millions of pounds in debt interest.

“Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith in it,” he said. “They are sick of seeing their waterways polluted, their bills going up, and drinking water gush through broken pavements while supplies run low. We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy-riding in the family car.

“The government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service. We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”

blocks.caption: Thames Water’s sewage treatment plant in Rickmansworth, Hertfordshire.  Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The report said ministers should explore all potential alternative options, including an SAR or using fresh legislation to draw a line under the debacle and restore stability to the sector by putting Thames Water on a sound footing for new buyers.

Carmichael said putting the company into special administration once its money ran out could be the only way to reset its fortunes. “Liabilities that the government will face in the short term may be offset by a future sale of Thames Water once a new buyer can be found,” he said.

The intervention comes after 64 MPs debated a 200,000-strong petition, set up by the campaigner Ash Smith of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, to hold a referendum on putting the privatised water industry back into public ownership.
MPs on the Efra committee said they were concerned that not enough regulatory due diligence had been carried out on the US-led consortium that bought Thames Water’s debt.

Elliott Investment Management is one of the leading creditors in the group that includes Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G. Elliott’s founder and co-chief executive is Paul Singer, a Trump donor whom Bloomberg has described as “the most feared investor in the world”.
after newsletter promotion

The consortium of hedge funds – known as London & Valley Water – is attempting to take over Thames in a multibillion-pound restructuring. It is seeking relief from environmental fines which could be worth up to £1bn, requesting leniency on environmental measures including pollution, leakage and other performance targets imposed a year ago.
MPs said: “Their demands demonstrate that they will not prioritise the swift turnaround in performance that Thames Water so desperately needs.

“Whilst keeping the company in limbo by drawing out negotiations, these creditors are simultaneously reaping millions in debt interest and fees. We have grave concerns … L&VW is an opaque consortium which is failing to live up to the transparency the public expects of the water sector.”

The committee said it was difficult to see why SAR had not already been instigated for Thames Water. “Thames Water is at the end of the road. The company’s performance and the behaviour of its creditors are unacceptable. Their investment strategies are based on extracting value through debt rather than ensuring long-term success.”

blocks.caption: Thames Water employees inspect damage after a burst pipe and flooding in south London. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s complex problems.

“The plan will write off billions of pounds of debt to achieve an investment grade rating and provide £10bn of new capital from experienced investors to improve and upgrade Thames Water’s infrastructure and clean up local rivers.

“All fines Thames Water faces will be paid, all profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.

“A new board with specialist expertise will oversee Thames Water’s transformation and work tirelessly to drive the turnaround and rebuild trust. We are committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve. This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water’s record capital investment programme can continue without disruption.”

articles.title: Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules
articles.summary:
Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed

The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy…

blocks.text: The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”.
One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”.

Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class.
Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”.

“Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties.

blocks.caption: Guy Hills. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian

blocks.text: He called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said.

On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache.
He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends.

“They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said.

Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat.

While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said.

blocks.caption: Chaand Singh. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian

blocks.text: Among the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.”

Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.”

blocks.caption: James Sleater. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian

blocks.text: What do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.”

Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”.

Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years.

“If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.”

People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said.

As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.”
It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.

articles.title: Prosecutors: We spoke on procedure, summary, not merits of Sara Duterte case
articles.summary: Members of the House prosecution team maintained Friday that their statements about the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte were not about merits of the case, covering only…

blocks.text: Members of the House prosecution team maintained Friday that their statements about the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte were not about merits of the case, covering only procedure and summary of what were already discussed in the proceedings.

Representative Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list and private counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. asserted this in responding to the show cause order issued by the Senate impeachment court, which asked them to explain why their recent statements did not violate the sub judice rule baring parties to the case from speaking on its merits.

"Rep. Ridon's public statements have been made in the course of performing his responsibilities as a member of the House Prosecution Panel, and pursuant to the prosecution's commitment tokeep the public informed of the status and progress of the impeachment proceedings," Ridon said in his answer to the show cause order.

"In making these statements, Rep. Ridon never intended to prejudge the case, influence the Senator-Judges, substitute public discussion for the evidence and arguments properly presented before the Honorable Court, or diminish the authority of the Honorable Court to determine the merits of the impeachment case," Ridon added.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero had issued a directive barring senator-judges, as well as counsels for both the prosecution and defense, from speaking publicly on the merits of Duterte's impeachment case.

He cited Rule 18 of the Senate Impeachment Rules, which provides that, “The Presiding Officer, the Members of the Senate, the prosecutors, the person impeached, and their respective counsel and witnesses shall refrain from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial.”
Tolosa, for his part, said his statements were mere explanation on how the prosecution intends to present its evidence before the Senate impeachment court.

"With due respect, none of the challenged statements falls within the prohibition under Rule 18. Some concerned only procedural matters and did not evaluate the merits of the case. The others merely recounted matters already placed on the public record during the proceedings, fairly and accurately, in good faith, and without editorial comment," Tolosa said.

"Accordingly, there is no basis for citing the undersigned counsel for violation of Rule 18. When each challenged statement of the undersigned counsel is considered in its complete context, none evaluates a disputed fact, the credibility of a witness, the relevance, weight, or sufficiency of evidence, the legal viability of an Article of Impeachment or substantive defense, or the proper disposition of any charge," Tolosa added.
Further, Tolosa said his statements did not state that the prosecution's evidence was already sufficient to warrant the Vice President's conviction.
Likewise, Tolosa said he did not urge the Senate impeachment court to convict the Vice President.

"A statement made to explain a procedural decision of the Prosecution: that it would no longer present its remaining witnesses because their testimony would be cumulative of matters already adduced during the hearings. It was not an assessment of the weight, probative value, or legal sufficiency of the evidence for purposes of conviction or acquittal," Tolosa said.

"The undersigned counsel did not assess the credibility, weight, or sufficiency of those statements and admissions, nor did he urge this Honorable Impeachment Court to draw any particular conclusion from it. Instead, it was merely made to explain the Prosecution's decision to reserve its right to call Respondent (Vice President) to address matters attributed to her in the evidence already presented," Tolosa added.

Tolosa said he merely summarized the argument put forward by his teammate, private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia, when the defense suddenly said the unusual names of the confidential fund recipient were alias only after three weeks of the impeachment trial when the defense never said these names were aliases in their verified answer to the impeachment case.

"The said statements are not comments but were accurate reiterations of the declarations previously made in open court by the witnesses of the prosecution and one of the counsels of the panel of prosecutors. Thus, a restatement of the same during the September 8 press conference clearly constitute fair and true reporting which is an exception to 18," Tolosa added. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Robin Padilla says he no longer has plans to run for public office
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla said Friday that he no longer has plans to run for public office as he seeks to live a peaceful life, adding that it is clear that he does not belong in politics.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 12:45pm
Senator Robin Padilla said Friday that he no longer has plans to run for public office as he seeks to live a peaceful life, adding that it is clear that he does not belong in politics.
“Maliliit pa ang aking mga anak, at isang tahimik na buhay-Islami ang aking pinapangarap at minimithi,” Padilla said in a Facebook post.
(My children are still young, and I dream and long for a peaceful Islamic life.)

He named Senators Alan Peter Cayetano, Imee Marcos, Christopher “Bong” Go, Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta, and former presidential chief legal counsel Salvador Panelo as his preferred running mates for Vice President Sara Duterte.
The senator expressed gratitude to his friends and supporters, but said, “halata naman po na hindi ako nababagay sa mundong ito.”
(It is clear that I do not belong in this kind of world.)

Padilla’s post came days after the Department of Justice issued a subpoena in connection with the complaint filed against him for obstruction of justice over Dela Rosa’s departure from the Senate amid an ICC warrant.
For his part, he maintained that he did not help Dela Rosa escape and that his colleague only hitched a ride in his car. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: BFAR vessel runs aground at Hasa-Hasa Shoal in West PH Sea --PCG
articles.summary: BFAR vessel runs aground at Hasa-Hasa Shoal in West PH Sea --PCG

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 12:31pm

A Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel on Thursday ran aground at Hasa-Hasa Shoal in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) during a fuel subsidy distribution, Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said Friday.
BRP Datu Magat Salamat was refloated after the PCG sent the BRP Malabrigo to assist, PCG spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said.

“Yesterday morning, while approaching a group of Filipino fishing vessels to position herself for the distribution of fuel to some 15 to 20 fishing boats, the vessel ran aground in the shallow waters of the shoal,” Tarriela said in a statement.
“The fishing boats immediately attempted to assist and provided initial towing assistance, but the effort was unsuccessful due to the morning low tide and their limited pulling power,” it added.
The BFAR vessel was at Hasa-Hasa Shoal to deliver fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen under the government's Kadiwa para sa Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda Program in the Kalayaan Island Group.
Initially, Filipino fishing boats tried to assist by towing the BFAR vessel but the effort was unsuccessful due to the morning low tide and their limited pulling capacity.
The PCG then dispatched BRP Malabrigo from Buliluyan Port in Bataraza, Palawan with Coast Guard divers on board.
BRP Malabrigo arrived at around noon and laid out a 600-meter towing line using its rigid-hulled inflatable boat.
“At around 3:34 PM, BRP Malabrigo safely pulled BRP Datu Magat Salamat out of the grounding area despite rough seas, southwesterly winds of 22 to 27 knots, and large waves,” Tarriela said.
Meanwhile, Tarriela said a China Coast Guard (CCG) aircraft with tail number 11101 was seen conducting aerial surveillance of the grounded BFAR vessel while the operation was underway. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Comelec pushes BSKE preparations pending new law; spending hits P8B so far
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) said on Friday that it will continue preparations for the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) while awaiting the passage of a law resetting the…

blocks.text: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) said on Friday that it will continue preparations for the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) while awaiting the passage of a law resetting the anticipated polls.

In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, Comelec Chairman George Erwin Garcia said preparations for the BSKE set on November 2 will continue, explaining that they need to be ready in case the bill fails to pass or is hit with a restraining order after enactment.
“Hindi po kami humihinto, Sir Melo, kasi hangga’t hindi ho nagiging batas ’yan, ang batas sa atin ay may eleksyon sa November 2,” Garcia said.
(We are not stopping, Sir Melo, because until that becomes a law, the existing law states that we have an election on November 2.)

“At pangalawa… napakahirap ipagbakasakali kasi kahit magkaroon ng batas, mero’t merong pupunta sa Korte Suprema at may posibilidad na biglang mag-issue ng restraining order… and therefore magtutuloy ang halalan sa November 2 pag nagkaganon ang sitwasyon,” he added.

(And second… it is too risky to take chances because even if a law is passed, someone will inevitably challenge it before the Supreme Court, and there is a possibility that a restraining order could be issued… which means the November 2 election would proceed under that scenario.)
On September 8, the House of Representatives approved House Bill 10971, which seeks to grant barangay officials a five-year term instead of the existing four-year term.
On September 14, the Senate passed Senate Bill No. 2387 on final reading, amending Republic Act No. 12232 to extend barangay and SK officials' terms from four to five years.
The measure also limits barangay officials to two consecutive terms in the same position and SK officials to one term.
The bill also proposes moving the next regular BSKE from the first to the second Monday of November 2028, with succeeding elections to be held every five years thereafter.
On September 16, the House plenary adopted the Senate bill to do away with the convening of the bicameral conference committee where lawmakers reconcile conflicting versions of the bills.
At this stage, only the approval and signature of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr is needed for the measure to be enacted into a law. The President can also reject or veto the bill.
Election lawyer Romy Macalintal has asked Marcos to veto the measure.
Garcia said Comelec has spent P8 billion on BSKE preparations so far. He noted that the preparations would not go to waste, as other materials can still be used if the BSKE is postponed to 2028.

“In all fairness, Sir Melo, hindi naman masasayang. Tayo po’y nakagastos na ng walong bilyong piso, natitira sa atin ay P11 billion na lamang, ‘yan po’y nasa kamay pa ng DBM (Department of Budget and Management) wala pa kay Comelec,” Garcia said.
(In all fairness, Sir Melo, it will not go to waste. We have spent eight billion pesos, leaving us with just P11 billion, which is still with the DBM and not yet with Comelec.)
“Pero 'yung mga na-imprenta nating mga balota, 'yung mga nabili naming ibang kagamitan, magagamit naman natin sa reset na barangay and sk elections kung saka-sakali,” he added.
(However, the printed ballots and other equipment we purchased can still be used in the rescheduled barangay and SK elections if ever.)
In anticipation of a possible delay, Garcia said they held off on having suppliers deliver certain materials to avoid compromising their quality, such as pens and indelible ink.
The poll chairman appealed for a prompt decision on the law, as the deadline for deployment of election materials nationwide nears should the BSKE proceed.

“Pero kinakailangan din po na merong desisyon kaagad kung tuloy o hindi sapagkat remember po, kinakailangan mag-deploy kami ng mga kagamitan sa mga unang linggo pa lamang ng Oktubre sa buong Pilipinas,” Garcia noted.
(There needs to be an immediate decision on whether it will proceed or not because remember, we need to deploy materials across the Philippines as early as the first week of October.)
The poll body said its preparations for the filing of certificates of candidacy (COCs) are also ongoing. The filing is scheduled for September 28 to October 5.

Meanwhile, the ban on public works and social services takes effect September 18, or 45 days before the elections. Garcia said this measure ensures that public funds are not used for personal campaign activities by candidates. —AOL, GMA News
