articles.title: Alex Ovechkin says he's 'for peace and love' after appearing in ad for Putin-aligned party
articles.summary: Alex Ovechkin says he's "for peace and love" after the Russian hockey star appeared in an ad for a party aligned with President Vladimir Putin during the off-season.

image.caption: Capitals star forward Alex Ovechkin previously voiced support for Russia's president in 2017 when he started a social movement called the 'Putin Team.' (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

blocks.text: NHL·New
Alex Ovechkin says he's "for peace and love" after the Russian hockey star appeared in an ad for a party aligned with President Vladimir Putin during the off-season.
'I'm Russian, and I support my country,' NHL star says
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Sep 17, 2026 4:22 PM EDT | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago

The video for the United Russia party came to light this week, days before Ovechkin's Washington Capitals held their annual media day Thursday. The NHL's career goal-scoring leader is back with the Capitals for a 22nd season.
Ovechkin is seen in the commercial standing behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Longtime Soviet hockey star Viacheslav Fetisov also participated.

"I'm Russian, and I support my country," Ovechkin said Thursday from Arlington, Va. "I'm for peace and love, and I hope in the world it doesn't matter who you are, I hope everybody understands everybody wants peace, and everybody hope everything's going to be OK in the world."
Ovechkin said he did not hesitate to participate in the ad.
"They asked me to do that. I say yes," he said. "So, it's as simple as that."
Ovechkin previously voiced support for the Russian president in 2017 when he started a social movement called the "Putin Team."
At the time, he told reporters from the AP and The Washington Post, "I just support my country."
Ovechkin appears in Putin campaign ad. NHL says nothing
'No more war,' Ovie pleaded in 2022

When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin said, "Please, no more war," when asked about the situation. Asked then about his relationship with Putin, Ovechkin said: "He's my president, but I'm not in politics. I'm an athlete."
Russia's parliamentary election this week features United Russia, plus nine others that all support Putin's policies. The only party that opposed the war in Ukraine has been barred from the ballot.

items: A look at Ovechkin's close ties to Putin
Ovechkin addresses Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022

blocks.text: Ovechkin, who turned 41 on Thursday, confirmed he plans to live in Russia when he retires from the NHL.

"I'm going to stay there. I'm going to live there, my kids are going to live there, family. So, I'm for peace and love, and I hope everything's going to be OK," Ovechkin said. "My home is Russia. DC is my second home. I have lots of friends.
“I grew up here as a person and I love DC. This is my second home. So I hope everything's going to be OK, and how I said — peace and love for everybody."

There was speculation last season would be Ovechkin's last, but he chose to stay with the Capitals for at least another year, and he remains noncommittal about what the future might hold after 2026-27.
"I'm focusing right now on training camp," Ovechkin said. "I have to make the team."

articles.title: Great Dane gets stretcher ride down B.C. mountain after injuring paws
articles.summary: A rough excursion for a very large dog and her two owners ended on a positive note last weekend, with a full-service stretcher ride down a mountain near Revelstoke, B.C.

image.caption: Revelstoke Search and Rescue was called to Mount Macpherson on Sept. 13, to assist a 10-year-old great dane who had torn her paw pads and could no longer make the trek back to the trailhead. (Revelstoke Search and Rescue)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A rough excursion for a very large dog and her two owners ended on a positive note last weekend, with a full-service stretcher ride down a mountain near Revelstoke, B.C.
Revelstoke SAR says owners couldn't carry pooch down themselves and wouldn't leave her behind
The 10-year-old, 120-pound Great Dane was out for a hike with her owners on Mount Macpherson on Sept. 13 when she tore her paw pads, according to Revelstoke Search and Rescue manager Ren Bassette.
"She was an angel," she said. "A 100 per cent good girl."

Bassette said the dog's owners didn't want to make the injuries worse and knew they couldn't carry their large pooch all the way out, so they activated the emergency SOS function on one of their phones.

items: Family of missing B.C. mountaineer believes she fell during Matterhorn descent
Art for arf’s sake! Micah Lexier launches multi-city art carnival for dogs (and their people)

blocks.text: Typically, Bassette said, the provincial government won't reimburse search and rescue teams for non-human rescues, but she said temperatures on the mountain were dropping rapidly and the owners needed urgent help too.
Bassette said the two weren't prepared to spend the night outside, and weren't willing to leave their dog behind.
Thankfully, another hiker stopped and lit a small fire for the owners and dog to keep warm as they waited for assistance, said Bassette.
"They were in good shape when we arrived."
Basette said their team bandaged the dog's paws and loaded her into a wheeled basket stretcher.
"She was so calm," said Bassette. "And she looks like she enjoyed the ride."
The owners walked out behind their chariot-riding dog, wearing extra clothes the search team had brought in.
Bassette said the team finally loaded the dog into her owners' vehicle around 1 a.m., and that all three are doing well.

articles.title: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak
articles.summary:
The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law

As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises,

blocks.text: As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly two decades.

“Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change.
“But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said.
He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once.

“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”

Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania.

Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”.

There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD.

Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government.
“We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday.

Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy.

“I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up the MMR into three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?”

Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy.
But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight.
“Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.”

The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection.
Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails.

He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now under investigation by their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authorities cancelled the project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers.
Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.”

Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said.

Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.”

Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action.

Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause.

articles.title: Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
articles.summary: People the BBC spoke to are excited by the prospect of working and studying in the EU, a suggestion Carney made this week.

blocks.text: Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with Europe
Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.
"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.

Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.
Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".

But before Canadians start packing their bags, "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.
Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.
Miriam Levin-Gold is excited about potentially greater opportunities for young Canadians to be able to explore the EU
Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.
"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.
Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.

One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.
"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.
The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.
Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.
"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.
But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.
"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe

blocks.text: David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe
Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.
"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."
For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.
"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.
"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."
These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.
Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.
Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US

blocks.text: Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US
The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.

A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.
However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.
A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.

"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US

blocks.text: Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US
And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.
"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.
Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."
But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.
"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."
With additional reporting by Madeline Halpert and James Fitzgerald

articles.summary: The lawyers of the drug war victims have asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to declare former President Rodrigo Duterte fit for trial.

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 3:51am
The lawyers of the drug war victims have asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to declare former President Rodrigo Duterte fit for trial.

The heavily redacted document submitted by Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda, the "Observations on behalf of the victims on the joint and individual reports of the panel of experts" was posted on the ICC a day after the third status conference that was attended by Duterte.

The Common Legal Representative of the Victims (CLRV) said that based on scientific conclusions, the legal criteria governing fitness to stand trial under the established jurisprudence of the Court are fully satisfied in the present case."
The CLRV also said, "Under the Court's jurisprudence, the absence of any impairment preventing the meaningful exercise of fair trial rights is determinative of fitness to stand trial."
The CLRV took note of the case of Mahamat Said Abdel Kani, a former general of the Central African Republic, on fitness to stand trial.

"As recently affirmed in the Said Case, the ability of an accused, viewed overall and in a reasonable manner, to understand and participate in the proceedings and to instruct counsel is central to a finding that they are fit to stand trial," the victims' lawyers said.

The lawyers added that as to the recommendation of the experts as to the attendance and participation of Duterte in the trial, "[REDACTED], the CLRV do not oppose the adoption of reasonable accommodations, provided that such measures do not prejudice the rights of other participants or the orderly conduct of the proceedings."
Earlier, the ICC prosecutor has asked Trial Chamber III to declare Duterte fit for trial.

In a document, posted on the ICC website and dated September 14, ad interim Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang submitted an observation on the Panel of experts' joint and individual reports after Duterte underwent a medical examination.
Niang also said that there is no statutory requirement for a hearing on Duterte's fitness to attend his trial is not necessary.
After the third status conference held on September 16, 2026, the ICC Trial Chamber III has unanimously decided to keep former President Rodrigo Duterte detained.

In a decision released shortly after the conclusion of the third status conference, the Chamber found a likelihood of Duterte “absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings.”

“In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists, (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” the decision read. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
articles.summary: Queensland's Fitzroy River has been selected for the 2032 Games, despite concerns over the course - and its inhabitants.

blocks.text: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.
Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".
The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

articles.title: Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases
articles.summary: Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and stricter regulations in Argentina, more and more Russians are choosing to travel to Brazil to give birth to children, who will obtain Brazilian…

image.caption: All women have access to public healthcare in a Brazil, regardless of visa or residency status Image: Felipe Dana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yulia and Dmitri (whose names have been changed for reasons of safety) flew from Russia to Brazil this summer so that their child could be born there. Yulia was 32 weeks pregnant at the time of travel.
"Of course, we didn't say that I was pregnant at border control," Yulia told DW.

Her daughter was born at a private clinic in Santos, a city in southern Brazil. Anybody born in the country has an automatic right to Brazilian nationality. The family is currently preparing all the paperwork.

"We've achieved our minimum goal," said Dmitri. "With a Brazilian passport, our daughter will be able to travel without a visa to almost any country in the world. She won't have to apply for an expensive and time-consuming Schengen visa. We want her to be able to decide for herself where she studies, works or lives."
He said that a colleague of his had traveled to Brazil in early August with his pregnant wife for the same reasons.

Yulia and Dmitri said that they had spent the equivalent of about €10,000 (about $11,500) during the first six weeks of their stay in Brazil, which included the costs for several days of treatment for their daughter in intensive care. Dmitri quit his job at a bank for the trip and hopes to find work again after the family returns to their home in the Russian capital Moscow.
However, they are only planning to return once all the documents for their daughter are ready and that could take months. Other Russian families have decided to stay in Brazil permanently.

According to organizations and lawyers that provide support to Russians in Brazil, there has been an increase in immigration from Russia, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after which visa requirements for Russian nationals entering certain countries were tightened.
Should EU countries grant fewer visas to Russians?
Argentina tightens visa regulations

Birth tourism to Brazil has also increased since Argentina, which used to be one of the main destinations for people wanting their children to be born in a country that automatically grants citizenship to newborns, tightened its regulations. People who want their children to obtain Argentinian citizenship now have to have resided in Argentina for at least two years. Since 2025, the access of people who do not have a permanent residence permit to free healthcare has also been restricted.
According to the Russian news outlet RBC, more than 7,000 Russians applied for a residence permit in Argentina in 2023. By mid-2025, the number had decreased to about 1,800.
Meanwhile, almost 500 Brazilian passports were issued to Russians in 2024 and more than 600 the following year. More than half of the new citizens were women.
The parents of a child born in Brazil can apply for a residence permit, which they can obtain within a year, under certain circumstances.

blocks.caption: Almost anybody born in Brazil can obtain Brazilian nationality Image: Paulo Lopes/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yana (name changed) and her husband chose to do this in 2023.

"The events of 2022 certainly played a role, but we had already toyed with the idea of giving birth abroad," Yana told DW. "A lot can happen in Russia. I always wanted a second passport and to give birth to my child in another country. When I became pregnant unexpectedly, all we had to do was decide which country made sense."
Yana gave birth to a boy at a public hospital in Florianopolis, the capital of the southern state of Santa Catarina, and the family stayed in Brazil for about three years.

"It was important to get passports for us and our child. I really enjoyed living there, and I learned Portuguese," Yana said, adding that she and her husband have lived as "digital nomads" in various countries over the years.

Even though they no longer live in Brazil, they want their son to have a connection to his birth country: "We read Portuguese books and talk a lot about Brazil. I want him to be able to travel without a visa and remain open to the world."
Big Russian community in Florianopolis

One of the largest Russian communities in Brazil lives in Florianopolis, and it's growing. According to the local health authorities, 119 Russian women took advantage of prenatal consultations in the first six months of this year. In all of 2025, it was 136 Russian women.

A lawyer who preferred to remain anonymous told DW that Brazil neither expressly prohibited nor permitted foreign nationals to enter the country for the purpose of giving birth. Often pregnant women do not disclose their reason for traveling to Brazil at border control. And once they are in the country they have access to free public hospitals and medical facilities regardless of their immigration status.

blocks.caption: Florianopolis is home to one of the largest Russian communities in BrazilImage: Anderson Coelho/DW

blocks.text: As Russian birth tourism to Brazil increases, a whole industry has emerged. Often, recent Russian immigrants to Brazil act as intermediaries and help others find housing or medical care. They provide assistance with complicated administrative procedures or the language. Depending on the level of care, the cost can reach into the thousands of dollars.

However, providers of such services, lawyers, and volunteers report stricter controls by Brazilian authorities, particularly in cities with larger Russian communities, such as Florianopolis. They say authorities are requesting more documents than in the past.

"The police are conducting more thorough checks to verify whether people actually live at the addresses they provide," one lawyer said, explaining that in the past, false addresses had been given by people hoping to obtain residence permits more quickly.
No evidence of Brazil systematically denying entry to Russians
But DW did not find any evidence to suggest that Russians were being denied entry to Brazil en masse.

In late July, the Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that 10 pregnant women had been "deported" from Russia. The information was later picked up by various media outlets. However, the Brazilian police denied the veracity of the report to DW, explaining that decisions to deny somebody entry to the country were always made on a case-by-case basis, and that pregnancy played no role in the process.

DW was only able to find one documented case of a pregnant Russian woman being initially refused entry into Brazil. She was allowed to enter the country after a lawyer intervened. According to the court records, the Brazilian border authorities had doubts as to how the Russian national would be financing her stay in Brazil.
The woman did not respond to the DW's inquiries.
This article was originally written in Russian.

articles.title: Barenaked Ladies set to sing O Canada at Buffalo Bills home opener tonight
articles.summary: The NFL's Buffalo Bills celebrated their Canadian fans with a game of cross-border catch, from boat to boat, floating along the Niagara River, the same day U.S. President ‌Donald Trump ​signed a…

image.caption: Buffalo Bills fans gather before the team's home opener against the Detroit Lions on Sept. 17, 2026. While trade tensions escalate between Canada and the U.S, the Bills celebrate their Canadian fans inviting Barenaked Ladies to sing O' Canada before the game. (Lauren Battagello/CBC)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

The NFL's Buffalo Bills celebrated their Canadian fans with a game of cross-border catch, from boat to boat, floating along the Niagara River, the same day U.S. President ‌Donald Trump ​signed a presidential ​memorandum aimed at removing Canadian-origin goods from U.S. civil service procurement.
The Buffalo Bills play the Detroit Lions in their 2026 home opener Thursday at 8 p.m. ET

On the day the White House said U.S. President ‌Donald Trump ​signed a presidential ​memorandum to ⁠identify ⁠Canadian-origin goods ‌in federal ⁠civil government procurement for the purpose of removing them, the NFL's Buffalo Bills celebrated their Canadian fans with a game of cross-border catch, from boat to boat, floating along the Niagara River.

Trump's memorandum signed Wednesday is the latest move in an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S. after talks fell apart last month. It came a week after he banned the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S.

items: Trump signs memorandum to identify and remove Canadian products from U.S. federal procurement
Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war

blocks.text: For the Bills, it's the latest effort to celebrate their Canadian fans in advance of their home opener tonight at 8 p.m. E.T., the first ever regular-season game at the team's new Highmark Stadium in Buffalo.

On Wednesday, the team posted a video on social media platform X showing retired Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick and retired wide receiver Stevie Johnson complete a few cross-border catches along the Niagara River, tossing to each other from aboard distant ferries.

Niagara Parks, the Ontario agency that manages the Canadian side of the Niagara River, said in a news release on Wednesday that the successful boat to boat passes "will be aired during NFL on Prime’s broadcast of the Buffalo Bills first 2026 home game on Thursday, September 17."
Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada

In the release, Kate Hussmann, Buffalo Bills Chief Strategy Officer, said “we’re thrilled to be part of such a unique event and to celebrate the connection we share with Bills fans across Southern Ontario. The passion and support we feel from our Canadian fans is incredible, and we look forward to continuing to deepen those relationships and create memorable experiences together for years to come.”
The agency said the Bills "participate in the NFL’s Global Markets Program, which grants the franchise official international marketing and fan engagement rights in Canada."

Last week, the team said on social media platform X that both O Canada and The Star-Spangled Banner will be performed before Thursday's home opener against the Detroit Lions and that the team "will celebrate the American and Canadian anthems during pregame." Actress and singer Auliʻi Cravalho will perform the American anthem and Toronto band Barenaked Ladies will sing O Canada.

The Canadian national anthem is rarely heard before NFL games, but it's commonly played before National Hockey League games in Buffalo, even when the Sabres are up against American opponents. In April, fans at KeyBank Center in Buffalo sang O Canada after a microphone failed before the Sabres' playoff game against the Boston Bruins.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Conrad Collaco is a CBC News producer for CBC Hamilton with extensive experience in online, television and radio news. Follow him on Twitter at @ConradCollaco, or email him at conrad.collaco@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Judge orders Kennedy Center to give 30-day notice before any major changes — including demolition
articles.summary: A U.S. federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30-day notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has…

image.caption: A tarp covers portions of the sign at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Wednesday. A judge has ordered the centre's board to give 30-day notice before making any major changes to the building. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30-day notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has threatened to do.
Ruling comes after board voted to close center after losing bid to put Trump's name back on it
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events," including the sudden closure of the building to the public on Wednesday.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said he closed the iconic performing arts centre temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building.
The building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration," Floca said.

The temporary closure, which occurred without notice Wednesday, is separate from a vote Tuesday by the Kennedy Center's board to close the performing arts centre indefinitely for repairs, Floca and other officials said. The closure was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he said.

The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by a Democratic congresswoman who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building's "unlawful closing."

Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building. Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.
Kennedy Center board votes to close after failed efforts to add Trump name | Hanomansing Tonight

Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning."

Cooper denied a request by Beatty's legal team to hold a hearing to clarify the board's actions and intent. But he agreed to their request "to make crystal clear" that his order prohibits demolition of the building.
The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the centre after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building.

Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, "because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape."
Congress has allocated $257 million US to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.
Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, on Thursday questioned the closing of the centre for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation "galling and painful to witness."

items: Fencing goes up around Kennedy Center as activists worry it will be demolished
Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge again blocks efforts to add Trump name to it

blocks.text: The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe Trump's name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also have been renamed in Trump's honour.
All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing."

Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution's leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump's name was once displayed.

articles.title: ‘I’m genuinely sorry’: Australian Hyrox athlete who soiled herself apologises to China and rivals
articles.summary:
• Joanna Wietrzyk ‘regrets’ decision to keep racing

  • She forfeits points from her win in the Beijing race

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.

Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk, said she offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.

Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record holder, went viral after it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.
But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there is “more to life than racing”.
“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.

“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”
Furhtermore, she said, she would forfeit the points from winning the event.

”I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”
Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It debuted in mainland China in late 2024.

In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

Ending her statement, Wietrzyk said: “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

articles.title: Who may continue receiving 4Ps aid beyond 7 years?
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said that the extension of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program"s (4Ps) maximum seven-year period will apply only to beneficiary families…

blocks.text: Published September 18, 2026 1:34am

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said that the extension of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program’s (4Ps) maximum seven-year period will apply only to beneficiary families classified under Level 1 (Survival) and Level 2 (Subsistence).
“The extension will apply only to Level 1 - Survival and Level 2 - Subsistence,” said DSWD Assistant Secretary Elaine Fallarcuna of the Conditional Cash Transfer Group.

Fallarcuna said qualified households may continue receiving 4Ps assistance beyond the previous seven-year limit, but they must still meet the program’s eligibility requirements and comply with its conditionalities on health, education and attendance at Family Development Sessions.

The latest Social Welfare and Development Indicator (SWDI) results show that 1,381,625 families are qualified for the extension. Of these, 1,744 are classified under Level 1, while 1,379,881 are under Level 2.
“We would like to emphasize that the extension is not automatic at mayroon pong reassessment ito, every year," Fallarcuna said.
Beneficiaries will undergo annual reassessment using the enhanced SWDI tool, which the DSWD uses to measure a family’s economic sufficiency and social adequacy.
“If a family will be in Level 3 [Self-Sufficient] already next year, the path of that family will be a ‘transition path’ and not on the extension path,” she said.
She added that beneficiaries may exit the program once they reach Level 3 or no longer have monitored children, regardless of how long they have been enrolled.
“It is not based on the number [of years]. It is based on the reassessment to be conducted every year,” Fallarcuna said.

The 4Ps was launched in 2008 and institutionalized through Republic Act No. 11310 in 2019. The program provides conditional cash transfers to poor households to support children’s health, nutrition and education. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: NASA satellite discovers a new crater on the moon that formed just 2 years ago
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

image.caption: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter discovered a large new crater that formed in 2024. (NASA/GSFC/Intuitive Machines)

blocks.text: Science·New
Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.
'This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation,' scientists write
The steep-sided hole — 222 metres across and up to 43 metres deep — is the solar system's biggest known impact crater carved out in recent times.
Such a large-scale event is estimated to occur only once every 132 years, researchers said, making this a treasure trove of information as NASA prepares to build a base for astronauts on the moon.

"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," the scientists wrote in one of two studies appearing on the subject Wednesday in the journal Science Advances.

NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) spotted the crater on the moon's near side in May 2024 soon after it was formed by an incoming fragment of an asteroid or comet. The moon strike escaped real-time detection by telescopes on Earth and in space.

LRO's wide-angle images were not identified in the crush of data until August 2025. The spacecraft gathered more detailed pictures last fall, followed by confirmation of the discovery early this year.
The crater is named for the late Thomas McGetchin, a former director of Houston's Lunar and Planetary Institute.
Like gardening
Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 2,400 kilometres across.

This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 100 kilometres. Dust and rocky soil were hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines. Robinson was the lead author for one of the studies.

items: Here's the mark a SpaceX rocket crash left on the moon
Astronauts' movement increased subsurface temperatures on the moon, study finds

blocks.text: A separate study identified a seven-kilometre-wide cold spot around the new crater, consistent with a loosening of the moon's topsoil. Co-author David Paige of the University of California, Los Angeles, likens it to gardening.

"We're now thinking of impacts as a way to garden the regolith — churning the sediments and putting stuff above that's usually below the surface," Paige said in a statement. (Regolith is the term for the loose, solid material on top of bedrock.)

The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 show that the moon's top two centimetres of soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years, faster than previously thought, according to Robinson.
Contrary to the popular belief that the Apollo moonwalkers' dusty lunar footprints will last forever, they will "definitely be long gone in that time frame," Robinson said in an email.
The next step is to calculate the risk of ejected crater material striking NASA's planned moon base, he added.
"That information will help engineers harden structures so one won't have to worry about damage, or maybe worry less."

articles.title: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump to raise arrest at Xi meeting
articles.summary: Sylvia Zin is among the family members of people imprisoned in China who are seeking Trump's help when he hosts the country's leader next week.

blocks.text: The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week.
U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference.
"I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday.
Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May.
Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release.

Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression.
In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years.

"Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said.
Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation."
Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit."

Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence.

The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one".
Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President."
Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China.

This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release.

Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive".
Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail.
"I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said.
Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request.

articles.title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
articles.summary: There is no certainty that the idea will ever get off the ground, let alone become a blueprint for other countries, writes Katya Adler.

blocks.text: Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.
The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.

But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."
Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.

The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.
Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.
The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.

"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.
Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.

This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.
Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.

Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".
But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.
Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU.

But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs.
They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.

Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.
For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.

But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.
Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.
No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.
A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.
Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.

In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

articles.title: A war-fatigued and anxious Russia picks a new parliament
articles.summary: Fuel shortages, drone strikes and mobilization rumors are fueling anxiety and war fatigue in Russia. As support for peace talks grows among Russians, the Kremlin is watching closely ahead of…

image.caption: The upcoming Duma elections are hard to miss when you walk down Moscow's streetsImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russians are increasingly anxious. Nearly half of those surveyed by state pollster FOM say a sense of alarm is the prevailing mood among the people around them.
According to data by independent pollster ExtremeScan, 60% of Russians believe that the war against Ukraine has had negative consequences for their day-to-day lives.
"Anxiety and war fatigue are driven by increasing uncertainty," Margarita Zavadskaya, a sociologist and senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs in Helsinki, told DW.

She says this year has seen a shift in public opinion. Rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and rumors of another mobilization drive are making it harder for Russians to plan for the future. Some are even leaving the country, afraid they could be drafted after the elections.

blocks.caption: All 450 seats in the Duma are at stake in the upcoming electionImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sociologist and the founder of ExtremeScan Elena Koneva said people were starting to ask the question: "How much does this war cost me and my family? And am I ready to pay this price? "
That could pose a problem for the Kremlin.

From September 18 to 20, Russians are voting for a new parliament (the State Duma) for the first time since 2022. It's the first parliamentary election to take place in Russia during the Ukraine war. And although there are unlikely to be any surprises in the official results, the Kremlin will be closely monitoring turnout.
Why are these elections important for the Kremlin?
"The Kremlin is confident it can fabricate whatever figures it needs. The question is how high of a price it will have to pay," said Zavadskaya.

Although elections in authoritarian systems like that of Russian President Vladimir Putin have little to do with democratic change, they still serve an important purpose. They are a reality check on whether the population remains loyal. And for Putin, that is especially important right now.

"They are crucial for him because they demonstrate that the majority supports the main party, the party of war, and that he has legitimacy for further escalation and the continuation of this war," Russian opposition politician in exile Ilya Yashin told DW.

In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, there is little sign the Kremlin is willing to end the conflict. United Russia, a party de facto led by Putin, is campaigning on a platform that lists victory in the war among its priorities. Its candidate list is headed by people presented as veterans of the war against Ukraine.
But many Russians appear to want the opposite.

"The silent majority just wants the war to end," opposition politician Yulia Galyamina, who still lives in Russia, said in a recent interview with online media-outlet Bereg. Most of these people still support Putin, but they are becoming increasingly anti-war, she said.

That mood is also reflected in polling. Six in 10 Russians favor peace negotiations with Ukraine, according to independent pollster Levada Center. Recent Kremlin hints at a new round of peace talks in October may be a tactic to calm the electorate, Zavadskaya said.
Support for Yabloko has been rising
One party has sought to capitalize on this anti-war sentiment: Yabloko.
The liberal opposition party is the only registered political force opposing the war in Ukraine.
Although its rating was below 5% in July, the party has seen a surge in popularity since then. Many people, especially younger Russians, are joining Yabloko and volunteering.
Russian court confirms anti-war party election ban

According to the independent pollster ExtremeScan, 18% of Russians would have voted for Yabloko. But they will not be able to: In a recent court decision, Yabloko was barred from running in the parliamentary elections.
"This support for Yabloko is, in fact, a demonstration of people's attitude toward the war," Koneva told DW.
What will anti-war voters do?
Now, with Yabloko out of the race, are there still ways for Russians to express that attitude?

Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Alexei Navalny, and opposition politician in exile Maxim Katz are urging supporters to back any party except United Russia in an effort to reduce the ruling party's result in the election.
Yabloko has taken a different approach, encouraging voters to spoil their ballots.
Yashin says neither choice matters. What matters, he says, is showing up at polling stations at noon on Sept. 20.

blocks.caption: Navalnaya (center) and Yashin (right) have different suggestions for how voters in Russia can show their discontent with the government (file photo from June 2025)Image: Alexis Haulot/European Union 2025 - Source : EP

blocks.text: "These queues will be a visible expression of public discontent," he said. "No need for flags, banners, or symbols. Everyone will know: the queues at noon are made up of people who do not want the war to continue."
DW Russian asked its readers anonymously whether they plan to vote in the upcoming election. Most of those who responded said they would follow Navalnaya's and Katz's advice.
"Elections have long become a farce and a political spectacle. But I will vote because I want to show that I have a position," one user said.
Others decided to stay away from the elections. One respondent wrote: "I don't want to legitimize Putin's regime."
Sergei Satanovskii contributed reporting.
